title: Driveway Surfacing
text:
Estimating materials needed for a simple gravel road, like my driveway.
A gravel road typically has three components: a layer of geotextile to prevent mixing the base with the substrate, a base layer of about 2” crushed rock to provide a foundation, and a surface layer of material that develops a hard surface. Each of the layers is 4 to 8” or so. A driveway will typically be about 12’ wide, and the surface must be sloped to prevent water pooling.
Gravel is generally ordered by weight (since the yards use scales rather than buckets). A ton of crushed rock / gravel is typically about \(1.4 ton.yd^{-3}\). A dump truck generally holds 22 ton, which equates to 15.7 yd. Crusher run includes the fines, and this is usally a bit heavier and variable by moisture content (best to order after a dry spell).
A one inch layer on a 12’ wide roadway is one cubic foot per foot of roadway. Since one cubic yard is 27 ft^3, one yard^3 will cover 27 ft, and one truck will cover about 424 ft at a one inch depth, 106ft at 4”, and 71ft at 6”.
The formula for tons per ft length per inch thckness is:
\[
\begin{eqnarray}
t &=& length \times 12 \times \frac{thick}{12 \times 27} \times 1.4 \\
&=& length \times thick \times 0.05185 \\
&=& \frac{length \times thick}{19.28}
\end{eqnarray}
\]
Assuming \(36 / ton, the cost per foot is:\)$ \[\begin{eqnarray}
cost &=& \frac{length \times thick}{19.28} \times 36 \\
&=& length \times thick \times 1.867
\end{eqnarray}\] $$
This comes out to around $1500 per one hundred feet of driveway at 8” thick, plus machine time and geotextile.

title: Catching Rain
text:
Collecting rainwater and storing it in a cistern for household use is not a novel concept. How much roof area and storage is needed? How should it be treated prior to consumption?
Rainwater was considered to be a generally clean source of water requiring minimal treatment for safe consumption (Thomas et al. 2014). A recent study (Cousins et al. 2022) reveals that PFAS contamination is now global, and untreated rainwater is no longer safe to drink anywhere on the earth. It is thus necessary to filter rainwater with a recommended process (US EPA 2018) for consumption. But what about the impacts of PFAS on the natural environment, with no luxury of filtration before consumption?
The average annual precipitation in Anne Arundel county is 42.45 inches, with an average of 4.17±0.25 per month with a 95% CI 1. Note that there is a lot of variability. May of 2015 was about 1.5 inches, June 2015 was over 12.5 inches of rain.
1 NOAA NCDC, Anne Arundel County

Code
import os
import json
import itables
import pandas as pd
import plotly.io as pio
import plotly.express as px

pio.renderers.default = "notebook"

data = []
dpath = "data/"
for m in range(1,13):
    with open(os.path.join(dpath, f"precip_{m}.json"), "r") as inf:
        mdata = json.load(inf)
        for k in mdata["data"].keys():
            year = int(k[:4])
            if year < 2021:
                month = m
                v = float(mdata["data"][k]["value"])
                row = [year, month, v]
                data.append(row)
df = pd.DataFrame(data, columns=["Year", "Month", "Precip"])
aaco_precip = px.scatter(
    df.query("Year < 2021").groupby(["Year"]).sum().reset_index(), 
    x="Year", 
    y="Precip",
    trendline="ols",
    labels={
        "Year":"Year",
        "Precip":"Precip. (in)"
    },
    height=400
)
aaco_precip.show()
stats = px.get_trendline_results(aaco_precip)
monthly_means = df.query("Year < 2021").groupby("Month").mean().reset_index()
monthly_std = df.query("Year < 2021").groupby("Month").std().reset_index()
monthly_precip = px.bar(
    monthly_means,
    x = "Month",
    y = "Precip",
    labels={
        "Month":"Month",
        "Precip":"Precip. (in)"
    },
    height=300,
    error_y=monthly_std["Precip"],
)
monthly_precip.update_traces(marker_color='rgb(158,202,225)', marker_line_color='rgb(8,48,107)',
                  marker_line_width=1.5, opacity=0.6)
monthly_precip.show()


        
        
        


                            
                                            


                            
                                            


The calculations are straight forward:
One inch is \(\frac{1}{12} ft\), so one inch of rain on one square foot of surface is:
\[
\frac{1}{12}ft \times 1ft \times 1ft = 0.08333ft^3
\]
Given \(1 gal = 231in^3\) and \(1ft^3 = 1728in^3\), so \(1ft^3 = 7.48049\:gal\) 2:
2 NIST Handbook 133. Appendix E. General Tables of Units of Measurement\[
1in = 0.08333 \times 7.48049 = 0.62337\:gal
\]
So one inch of rain on one square foot of surface yields 0.62337 gallons.
A household will use about 125 gallons per day with no deliberate conservation3. That equates to about 45,625 gallons per year. Assuming an average of 42.5” rain for the year in this part of Maryland, a catchment area of about 1800 sqft will be sufficient, more or less. Variability in input (rainfall) and output (use) is quite high, so storage buffering is necessary to get through the high use, low rainfall periods.
3 The range is is large, up to about 650 g/day, with median of about 125.

title: Fundamental SPO Operations
text:
Exploring some core operations on subject, predicate, and object combinations, i.e. RDF statements[^1].
Given a subject and predicate, what is the object?
Given a predicate and object, what is the subject?
Given a subject and object, what are the predicates?
Given a subject, what are the predicates?
Given a subject, what are the objects related by any predicate?
Given an object, what are the known predicates?
Given an object, what are the known subjects?

title: Innate Tendencies
text:
What are the fundamental dimensions of behavior?
People tend to prefer additive rather than subtractive changes (Adams et al. 2021).
People habitually seek order and consistency (Brotherton 2015). This desire for order may conflict with our preference for additive changes.
Humans are quite good at finding patterns. So much so, that we can find patterns where there are none (Friedman 2020). The tendency to find patterns where none exist can be exacerbated by a situation of disorder and conflict (Brotherton 2015).
Some people have a willingness to believe in unseen, intentional forces and an attraction to Maichean narratives1, Oliver and Wood 2014.
1 A tendency to look at things as having two sides that are opposed.When overwhelmed with information we have a tendency to simplify by reliance on paranormal or supernatural beliefs. It is something of a coping mechanism.
Paranormal belief scale: A belief in ghosts or extra sensory perception. See Louisiana Tech University and Tobacyk 2004
Supernatural belief scale: A belief in angels or the Devil (Jong, Bluemke, and Halberstadt 2013; Bluemke et al. 2017).
Creating a to-do list can result in more mind-wandering, suggesting that cues related to personal goals and concerns can trigger mind-wandering in a habitual stimulus-response-like fashion (Zedelius, Gross, and Schooler 2018, pp366). However, Masicampo and Baumeister 2011 found that making a plan for addressing the unresolved goals (rather than merely listing them) can free us from this kind of habitual mind wandering. Instead of merely listing things to be done, make the effort to determine how and when they are to be done, that is, plan the outcome ready for execution.

In chaotic situations, a tendency to follow those appearing to be more in control. (Is this a Trump control factor - create chaos and appear to be on top of the situation)

title: Identifiers
text:
An identifier is a sequence of characters used to identify a resource.
A resolvable identifier is an identifier which, when provided to a resolving service, provides the location of the identified resource. There are many implementations of resolver services, most mated to particular types of identifier, or identifiers that conform to a particular scheme.
Identifiers are generally composed of several components:
\(\color{navy}{\mathtt{Scheme}}:\color{salmon}{\mathtt{NAA}}/\color{red}{\mathtt{Prefix}}\color{darkorange}{\mathtt{Value}}\color{lightblue}{\mathtt{Extra}}\)
\(\color{navy}{\mathtt{Scheme}}\) indicates the type of identifier, for example “doi”, “ark”, and “igsn”.
\(\color{salmon}{\mathtt{NAA}}\) is an “Name Assigning Authority” which is a string (generally numeric characters) identifying the agent responsible for creating the identifier. Name assigning authorities are registered with the identifier infrastructure for the scheme.
\(\color{red}{\mathtt{Prefix}}\) is a set of characters at the start of the identifier value that can be used by a name assigning authority to group identifiers. This can be useful where parallel activities may be occurring (to avoid identifier collisions) or for grouping activities such as expeditions or experiments. Note that for legacy IGSNs, the prefixes are collaboratively managed to be unique across all name assigning authorities.
\(\color{darkorange}{\mathtt{Value}}\) is the part of the identifier that is specific to a single resource within the context of a scheme, name assigning authority, and prefix combination.
\(\color{lightblue}{\mathtt{Extra}}\) includes any characters beyond the minted identifier. These offer no value in resolving an identifier, but a resolver should pass these characters verbatim to the resource provider.
Namespace = \(\color{salmon}{\mathtt{NAA}}/\color{red}{\mathtt{Prefix}}\).

Conspiracy
text:
Participants who were more likely to detect order in this [computer generated random sequence of coin tosses] sequence were also more prone to endorse belief in conspiracies Friedman 2020.

It should not surprise us that so many of our patients are vulnerable to medical misinformation and to “fake news” in general. Because of social media and the Internet, we are practically drowning in information. For a species so intent on connecting the dots and making sense of the world, this information-rich environment is fertile ground for confusion and conspiracy theories. People do not instinctively fact-check what they read or listen to—doing so requires far too much cognitive work and runs counter to how the brain has evolved. (Friedman 2020)

Research shows that higher levels of education are inversely correlated with belief in conspiracies, presumably because education fosters critical thinking and skepticism, which makes it easier to suppress one’s often misleading intuition (Prooijen 2017).
Conspiracy theories are a human reaction to confusing times. “We’re all just trying to understand the world and what’s happening in it,” says Rob Brotherton, a psychologist at Barnard College and author of Suspicious Minds: Why We Believe in Conspiracy Theories (Brotherton 2015).
conspiracy theory noun. “a theory that explains an event or set of circumstances as the result of a secret plot by usually powerful conspirators”
Conspiracy is the creation of belief or understanding from the incorrect interpretation of apparent patterns and associations to have factual basis.
People are unable to fact check large volumes of information, and instead tend to rely on pattern detection to form understanding.
Conspiracies gain traction through communication between like minded participants. Tribal behavior. Internet fora facilitate tribe formation.
An environment with overwhelming information leads to greater propensity for conspiracy theories to emerge.

Conspiracy theories contain contradictions.
Contention is based on shaky assumptions.
Interpreting evidence against as evidence for it.


Heath and Gifford 2006
Lewandowsky, Oberauer, and Gignac 2013

Suppression of education fosters a population more readily manipulated through belief in conspiracies. Information overload can further promote conpiratory belief.

title: DOIs are Borken. Sort of.
text: The current DataCite DOI resolver services does not respect content negotiation for JSON-LD. Instead of returning the location of the requested resource, the location of DataCite specific content is returned. The consequence is that the DataCite DOI infrastructure will not reliably resolve JSON-LD resources.

title: DOIs are Borken. Sort of.
text:
The problem
Implementation of content negotiation by DOI resolver implementations can override the functionality of a resource provider creating unpredictable results for a resource consumer.
For example, the DOI 10.1594/PANGAEA.930327 identifies a resource located at the URL https://doi.pangaea.de/10.1594/PANGAEA.930327. Requesting this resource over HTTP using an Accept header preferring text/html results in the HTML representation of the resource. When requesting the resource from that URL with a preference of application/ld+json, the resource provider returns a JSON-LD representation of the resource. This is the expected behavior.
If however a resource consumer performs DOI resolution to determine the location of the resource then the behavior is different. The DOI resolver will instead present the location of the resolver implementation copy of metadata (e.g. DataCite metadata). This means DOIs can not be used to reliably reference some content types. The list of content types overridden by DataCite includes:



Format
Content Type




RDF XML
application/rdf+xml


RDF Turtle
text/turtle


Citeproc JSON
application/vnd.citationstyles.csl+json


Schema.org in JSON-LD
application/ld+json


Codemeta
application/vnd.codemeta.ld+json


Formatted text citation
text/x-bibliography


RIS
application/x-research-info-systems


BibTeX
application/x-bibtex


DataCite XML
application/vnd.datacite.datacite+xml


DataCite JSON
application/vnd.datacite.datacite+json


JATS
application/vnd.jats+xml

title: DOIs are Borken. Sort of.
text:
Example
The following example illustrates the issue for the case of JSON-LD (a common serialization of schema.org RDF).
A request to resolve the HTML representation behaves as expected (> and < denote request and response respectively):
> https://doi.org/10.1594/PANGAEA.930327 
> Accept: text/html
< 302

title: DOIs are Borken. Sort of.
text:
Suggested fix
The DOI resolver service should respond with a resolver service metadata content representation only when specifically requested.
RFC 8288 provides a mechanism for advertising the availablity of related resource, including alternate representations of a resource aligned with different profiles.Web Linking defines a model for the relationships between resources on the Web (“links”) and the type of those relationships (“link relation types”).
The resolver can advertise an alternate representation of a resource by including such information in the HTTP response Link header. Similarly, a resource provider could also promote availability of the resolver metadata by presenting the location of such a representation in its response.
At a minimum such information should be included when a resolver returns an alternate representation of a resource not specifically presented by the resource authority.
Ideally, the DOI resolver should only respond with information about the location of the requested resource.
For example the DOI resolver could respond similarly to the following example, with the redirect response including a link to the location of the resolver metadata:
> https://doi.org/10.1594/PANGAEA.930327 Accept:application/ld+json
< Link: <https://data.crosscite.org/10.1594%2FPANGAEA.930327>; rel="alternate"; type="application/ld+json"; profile="http://datacite.org/schema"
< 302 https://doi.pangaea.de/10.1594/PANGAEA.930327

> https://doi.pangaea.de/10.1594/PANGAEA.930327 Accept:application/ld+json
< 200 application/ld+json
Note however that link header handling in redirect responses would only be available to programmatic clients. Intermediate communication details are not exposed to web browser based clients.

title: Identifier Resolution
text:
The practice of resolving an identifier to a resource location generally involves progressive refinement of location detail gathered through sequential inquiry to different sources of information. When resolution is performed over HTTP, the progressive refinement occurs through a series of HTTP redirects until the resource is located or the resolution is rejected as invalid.
The different sources of information about identifiers can be broadly grouped into three levels: Scheme Resolver, Prefix Resolver, and Resource Resolver.

The Scheme Resolver directs requests to services appropriate for a particular scheme (e.g. ark: or doi:). For example, a Scheme Resolver would have knowledge that identifiers following the “doi” scheme may be resolved by the service located at “https://doi.org/”. Similarly, ARK identifiers may be resolved at “https://n2t.net/”. A Scheme Resolver redirects an identifier resolve request to a known Prefix Resolver.
The Prefix Resolver supports grouping of identifiers with particular services. The Prefix Resolver typically examines a portion of the identifier such as a prefix to determine which services can provide more detail about the identifier. For example, ARK identifiers have a numeric prefix, the “NAAN” (Name Assigining Authority Number). Each NAAN is associated with a service responsible for managing identifiers created with that prefix. A Prefix Resolver redirects an identifier resolve request to a known Resource Resolver.
A Resource Resolver is able to associate an identifier with the location of a specific resource, which will generally be a Resource Server where the actual resource is stored and made available. A Resource Resolver service takes an identifier as input, and returns the Resource Server location information to the client.

The three levels of resolution described here is a broad generalization. Fewer or more levels may actually be involved in the resolution of any particular identifier. However, three levels has emerged as a somewhat typical pattern for scalable resolution of globally unique identifiers and provides a useful framework for discussion.
An example of sequential location refinement for resolution of the ARK identifier ark:/12148/bpt6k10733944 is provided in ?@fig-resolvers.



Generalization of identifier resolution through three levels of resolver service. The Scheme Resolver understands “ark:” identifiers are resolved by the Prefix Resolver n2t.net, which in turn understands identifiers with the prefix “12148” are resolved by the Resource Resolver ark.bnf.fr. The Resource Resolver in turn directs the user to the actual resource.


Note that there may be multiple instances of Scheme, Prefix, and Resource Resolvers. Where content between instances overlaps, it is critical that mechanisms are in place to ensure trustworthy consistency across instances. If knowledge of identifier detail was not consistent across resolver instances, resolution would produce inconsistent results, and so reduce the value of globally unique, resolvable identifiers. Service trustworthiness is important to avoid potential content spoofing or malicious action where an agent deliberately causes resolution to content different from content owner intent (E.g. an identifier pointing to a factual news article redirected to fake news by a malicious agent).
When expressing an identifier as a URL, the identifier is being directly coupled to a service, and so consideration should be given to the availability of the service and efficiency of use within the applicable context. In general, services at the finer level of detail in the resolver chain may be more ephemeral. Server names and url patterns may change as services evolve, and so URLs associated directly with those services may be considered somehwat more fragile in the long term. Hence, there is some benefit to constructing URLs using services at higher levels in the resolution chain.
There is no universal, globally accepted identifier scheme resolver service, though such capability is offered by identifiers.org and n2t.net. In the example workflow presented in Figure 1. above, any of the following URLs ultimately resolve to the same resource:

https://n2t.net/ark:/12148/bpt6k10733944
https://ark.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k10733944
https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k10733944

URL 3 is most closely associated with the resource, is more efficient for the user (no redirects), though may be more ephemeral and impacted by changes to the collection infrastructure. URL 3 could be considered appropriate for use within the collection viewer application where any future changes to the URL may be managed by the application logic.
At the other extreme, URL 1 might be considered good for long term reference to the resource. Retrieval of the resource is less efficient since there are more redirects, but is arguably more resilient to changes to underlying services since the resolver metadata may be updated as necessary by the resource managers, thus removing the need to change published URLs.

title: UnFAIR
text:
Unexpected consequences of academic altruism.
An interesting article on recognition of data contributors, “Time to Recognize Authorship of Open Data” 2022. Open data contributors (those offering their data for free via public services) were more likely to be listed as contributors than authors. Closed data contributors were more likely to be listed as authors. Hence, there is an incentive to not openly share data, since doing so decreases opportunity for being recognized as an author, and authorship is a more valuable recognition than contributor.
doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-022-00921-x
Those that do not make their data public are more likely to be authors on papers using the data than those that make their public. The later are more likely to be listed as contributors.
Thus there is an anti-incentive for sharing data publicly following the FAIR and data citation guidelines.




References

“Time to Recognize Authorship of Open Data.” 2022. Nature 604 (7904): 8–8. https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-022-00921-x.

text: Centimeter resolution GPS for under $500.

title: Precision GPS on the Cheap
text:
Base station
The sensor is positioned 12.91’ above the ground elevation of 144’, so the sensor is 156.91’ or +43.89m relative to MSL.
Coordinates are: +39.02699072 -76.56399835 +17.413m relative to the WGS-84 ellipsoid, 1152839.1256, -4825659.9491, 3994656.1792 m in ECEF. (+47.826m relative to MSL). In this region, MSL is approximately +13.71m relative to the ellipsoid.

title: Precision GPS on the Cheap
text:
Coordinate Conversion
Google maps, default GPS, and generally most common maps use WGS84 (latitude and longitude), which is EPSG:4326.
Earth-centered Earth-fixed coordinates are used for RTK reference and internally by things like Cesium. This is EPSG:4978.
The local coordinate system used by surveyors and legal documents is Maryland NAD83, which is EPSG:2893.
Converting to and from WGS84 (EPSG:4326) can be done using proj and most conveniently, the included cs2cs tool.
From WG884 (EPSG:4326) to NAD83 (EPSG:2893):
echo "39.02699653 -76.56401381" | cs2cs -f "%.5f" epsg:4326 epsg:2893
1436190.80285 495708.94613 0.00000
From NAD83 to WGS84:
echo "1436190.80285 495708.94613 0.00000" |  cs2cs -f "%.8f" epsg:2893 epsg:4326
-76.56401381 39.02699653 0.00000000
From WGS84 to ECEF:
echo "39.02699653 -76.56401381 47.826" | cs2cs -f "%.5f" epsg:4326 epsg:4978
1152843.21890   -4825682.84520 3994675.83102
From ECEF to WGS84:
echo "1152843.21890 -4825682.84520 3994675.83102" | cs2cs -f "%.8f" epsg:4978 epsg:4326
39.02699653 -76.56401381 47.82599962

title: Precision GPS on the Cheap
text:
Computing an offset
Convert the longitude, latitude to NAD83, adjust the easting, northing by the required amount (NAD83 is ft east-west and north-south), then convert the value back to longitude, latitude.
For example, the original base station estimate is about 1.2m off according to a couple reference points. The adjustmet is:
